I downloaded it (Internet Archive copy of the sil.org PDF; live site returns a not reachable by automated download), scanned it, and read the stress passages on the page images: p.2 'Stress is.. generally predictable. Penultimate stress is found in the great majority of the words'; sec. 5.3.1 p.23 'Stress and tone are not considered to be phonemic at the word level. In isolation, the majority of words have penultimate stress, and high tone usually occurs on the stressed syllable', with six stress-marked examples, all penultimate; sec. 7.1 p.27 'tendancy to conform to the penultimate stress rule' a

Manuscript, SIL, Ukarumpa. 37 pp. (SIL Language & Culture Archives entry 51990; posted 2009 'as is'). downloaded via the Internet Archive id_ copy of sil.org reapdata PDF (live URL an automated-access block-403); image-only PDF, scanned (tesseract, 200 dpi) to.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: p.2: 'Stress is not usually written, since it is generally predictable. Penultimate stress is found in the great majority of the words. When it is necessary to write stress, a ' is placed before the stressed syllable.' p.23: 'Stress and tone are not considered to be phonemic at the word level. In isolation, the majority of words have penultimate stress, and high tone usually occurs on the stressed syllable.' (examples p.23-24 all penultimate: 'isag, a'liga, wam'bele?w, ona'howa, kopisia'howa, alupu'tina). p.27: 'Stress placement on the vowels of a complex nucleus is usually distributed about e
sources.locator: Introduction, printed p.2 (PDF p.3); sec. 5.3.1 'Phonemic status of tone, stress, length', printed pp.23-24 (PDF pp.24-25); sec. 7.1, printed pp.26-27 (PDF pp.27-28)
sources.note: The primary phonology write-up behind the 4-page 1992 OPD our classification quotes; has a dedicated suprasegmentals section (5.3.1) with stress-marked examples and a phonological-word definition ('one and only one stress'). downloaded now; confirms penultimate, non-phonemic stress.
